# Background

Error-in-variables (EIV) models are useful tools to account for measurement error in the independent variable. For studies of agreement, this is particularly useful where there are paired measurements of the paired measurements (X & Y) of the same underlying value (e.g., two assays of the same analyte).

Deming regression is one of the simplest forms of of EIV models promoted by [W. Edwards Deming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Edwards_Deming)^[Deming was a titan of the fields of statistics and engineering and I would highly recommend reading some of his academic work and books]. The first to detail the method were @adcock1878 followed by @kummell1879 and @koopmans1936. The name comes from the popularity of Deming's book [@deming1943], and within the field of clinical chemistry, the procedure was simply referred to as "Deming regression" (e.g., @linnet1990). 

# Deming Regression

## Simple Deming Regression

We can start by creating some fake data to work with.

```{r}
library(SimplyAgree)

dat = data.frame(
  x = c(7, 8.3, 10.5, 9, 5.1, 8.2, 10.2, 10.3, 7.1, 5.9),
  y = c(7.9, 8.2, 9.6, 9, 6.5, 7.3, 10.2, 10.6, 6.3, 5.2)
)
```

Also, we will assume, based on historical data, that the measurement error ratio is equal to 2 (i.e., the error variance of x is twice the error variance of y).

The data can be run through the `dem_reg` function and the results printed. 

```{r}
dem1 = dem_reg(y ~ x,
               data = dat,
               error.ratio = 2,
               weighted = FALSE)
dem1
```

The resulting regression line can then be plotted. 

```{r}
plot(dem1, interval = "confidence")
```

## Model Diagnostics

The assumptions of the Deming regression model, primarily normality and homogeneity of variance, can then be checked with the `check` method for Deming regression results. Both plots appear to be fine with regards to the assumptions.

```{r}
check(dem1)
```

## Fitted Values and Residuals

After fitting a Deming regression model, you can extract the estimated true values and residuals. The `fitted()` function returns the estimated true Y values, accounting for measurement error. The `residuals()` function returns the optimized residuals by default, which correspond to the perpendicular distances from each point to the regression line.

## Weighted Deming Regression

For this example, I will rely upon the "ferritin" data from the `deming` R package.
`r if (!has_deming) "*The code in this section was not run because the deming package is not installed.*"`

```{r, eval = has_deming}
library(deming)
data('ferritin')

head(ferritin)
```

Let me demonstrate the problem with using simple Deming regression when the weights are helpful. When we look at the two plots below, we can see there is severe problem with using the "un-weighted" model.

```{r, eval = has_deming}
dem2 = dem_reg(
  old.lot ~ new.lot,
  data = ferritin,
  weighted = FALSE
)
summary(dem2)

plot(dem2)

check(dem2)
```

Now, let us see what happens when `weighted` is set to TRUE.

```{r, eval = has_deming}
dem3 = dem_reg(
  old.lot ~ new.lot,
  data = ferritin,
  weighted = TRUE
)
summary(dem3)

plot(dem3)

check(dem3)
```

The weighted model provides a better fit.

# Passing-Bablok Regression

Passing-Bablok regression is a robust, nonparametric alternative to Deming regression for method comparison studies [@passing1983]. Unlike Deming regression, it makes no assumptions about the distribution of the measurement errors. The method estimates the slope as the shifted median of all pairwise slopes between data points, which makes it resistant to outliers.

## When to Use Passing-Bablok

Passing-Bablok regression is particularly useful when:

- Both X and Y are measured with error
- You want a robust method not sensitive to outliers
- The relationship is assumed to be linear
- X and Y are highly positively correlated

## Basic Usage

The `pb_reg()` function implements three variants of Passing-Bablok regression:

- **"scissors"** (default): Most robust, scale-invariant method from @bablok1988
- **"symmetric"**: Original method from @passing1983
- **"invariant"**: Scale-invariant method from @passing1984

```{r}
# Create example data
pb_data <- data.frame(
  method1 = c(69.3, 27.1, 61.3, 50.8, 34.4, 92.3, 57.5, 45.5, 33.3, 60.9,
              56.3, 49.9, 89.7, 28.9, 96.3, 76.6, 83.2, 79.4, 51.7, 32.5,
              99.1, 14.2, 84.1, 48.8, 61.5, 84.9, 93.2, 73.8, 62.1, 98.6),
  method2 = c(69.1, 26.7, 61.4, 51.2, 34.7, 88.5, 57.9, 45.1, 33.4, 60.8,
              66.5, 48.2, 88.3, 29.3, 96.4, 77.1, 82.7, 78.9, 51.6, 28.8,
              98.4, 12.7, 83.6, 47.3, 61.2, 84.6, 92.1, 73.4, 61.9, 98.6)
)

# Fit Passing-Bablok regression
pb1 <- pb_reg(method2 ~ method1, data = pb_data)
pb1
```

## Summary and Plots

The summary provides details about the regression coefficients and diagnostic tests:

```{r}
summary(pb1)
```

The `plot()` method displays the regression line with data:

```{r}
plot(pb1)
```

## Model Diagnostics

The `check()` method provides diagnostic plots specific to Passing-Bablok regression, including the CUSUM linearity test and Kendall's tau correlation:
 
```{r}
check(pb1)
```

## Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

For more robust inference, especially with the "invariant" or "scissors" methods, bootstrap confidence intervals are recommended:

```{r}
pb2 <- pb_reg(method2 ~ method1, 
              data = pb_data, 
              replicates = 999)
summary(pb2)
```

# Bivariate Least Squares (BLS and CBLS)

`bls_reg()` implements the bivariate least squares regressions of @francq2014 and @francq2016, as in the BivRegBLS package. Like Deming regression, BLS allows for measurement error in both methods, but it uses the error variances themselves, known from a validation study (`var_x`, `var_y`) or estimated from replicates (`id`), rather than only their ratio. Each subject's mean is weighted by the error variance of that mean, so subjects with more replicates count for more, and the variances may differ between the methods. With constant variances, BLS gives the same line as Deming regression with `error.ratio = var_x / var_y`.

Because the variances are known, BLS also gives exact standard errors (without the jackknife) and **prediction intervals**: where a new measurement by one method is expected to fall, given a new measurement by the other.

```{r}
data("reps")
bls1 <- bls_reg(y ~ x, data = reps, id = "id")
summary(bls1)
predict(bls1, newdata = c(4, 6), interval = "prediction")
```

The same line can be fitted in the Bland-Altman plot (differences `x - y` against means). There, the errors of the differences and of the means are correlated whenever the two methods have different error variances, which an ordinary regression of the differences on the means ignores (see `vignette("method_conversion")`). Correlated BLS (CBLS) accounts for this [@francq2016]; it is reported with the BLS fit and drawn by `plot(type = "md")`. A slope of zero in this plot means a constant bias.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
plot(bls1, interval = "prediction")
plot(bls1, type = "md", interval = "prediction")
```

When the error grows with the level, as is common for laboratory measurements with a roughly constant coefficient of variation, the error variances can be given as functions of the level, or estimated from the replicates with `var_model = "proportional"` (constant CV) or `"power"`. The variances are then evaluated at each subject's estimated true values, and the prediction intervals widen with the level:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
data("ba1986")
bls2 <- bls_reg(mini1 ~ wright1, data = ba1986,
                 var_x = function(level) (0.05 * level)^2,
                 var_y = function(level) (0.07 * level)^2)
predict(bls2, newdata = c(200, 600), interval = "prediction")
plot(bls2, interval = "prediction")
```

In simulations, ignoring proportional error (`var_model = "constant"`) gave 95% prediction intervals that covered every new measurement at low levels but only about 81% at high levels.

Two other ways to describe the error are available. When each subject's error variance is known separately (for example, from that subject's replicates in an earlier study), `var_x` and `var_y` can name columns of the data holding them, with `df_var_x` and `df_var_y` naming columns of their degrees of freedom; this reproduces BivRegBLS's `BLS.ht()`. A new measurement is then given the mean of the subjects' variances. When the error SD is proportional to the level, `transform = "log"` fits the line to the logarithms, `log(y) = b0 + b1 log(x)`, with constant error variances on the log scale. `predict()` and `plot()` back-transform: fitted values and limits for `y` in the plot of `y` against `x`, and ratios `x / y` against the geometric mean in the Bland-Altman plot.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
bls3 <- bls_reg(mini1 ~ wright1, data = ba1986, error.ratio = 1,
                 transform = "log")
bls3
plot(bls3, type = "md")
```

BLS assumes that the measurement errors explain all the scatter about the line. `summary()` reports the **dispersion**, which should be near 1, with a test. A dispersion clearly above 1 means that the subjects' true values deviate from the line (equation error, e.g. matrix effects: one method reading some samples high for reasons the replicates cannot reveal). By default (`equation_error = TRUE`), these deviations are estimated, assuming the same variance for both methods (as `method_vc(tau = "common")`), and included in the fit and the prediction intervals; otherwise the prediction intervals would be too narrow. With two methods, the data cannot show how the deviations divide between the methods, so the slope depends on that assumption [@carstensen2010].

`joint_test()` tests intercept 0 and slope 1 with the Wald statistic from the BLS variance-covariance matrix; `predict(interval = "band")` and `plot(interval = "band")` give the corresponding simultaneous confidence band for the whole line, which contains exactly the lines the joint test does not reject. `check()` shows the standardized residuals. The estimates, standard errors, and confidence and prediction intervals reproduce BivRegBLS; its joint test multiplies the critical value by a Hotelling factor, $(n - 1)/(n - 2)$, so its p-values are slightly larger. The CBLS prediction intervals here also include the covariance between the errors of a new difference and a new mean, which BivRegBLS leaves out (the two agree when the error variances are equal).

## When the error ratio is unknown

Without replicates or a validation study, the error ratio needed by Deming regression is often a guess. `error_ratio_profile()` refits the line for every ratio from 0 (all error in `y`: ordinary least squares of `y` on `x`) to infinity (all error in `x`: least squares of `x` on `y`), as BivRegBLS's `FullCIs.XY()` does [@francq2014]. The **full confidence intervals** are the values of the slope and intercept that the data do not exclude whatever the ratio. When they exclude identity, or the joint test rejects it at every ratio, the conclusion does not depend on the guess.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
prof <- error_ratio_profile(dem_reg(mini1 ~ wright1, data = ba1986))
prof
plot(prof)
```

For the peak flow data, the slope moves only from 0.92 to 1.03 over all ratios, and identity is not rejected at any of them. The exact interval for the slope [@creasy1956] is shown when every subject has the same number of replicates by each method.

# Joint Confidence Regions

An experimental enhancement to the `dem_reg` and `pb_reg` functions is the addition of **joint confidence regions** for the slope and intercept parameters. Traditional confidence intervals treat each parameter separately, but in regression analysis, these parameters are correlated.

Joint confidence regions account for this correlation with a region in the (intercept, slope) parameter space. This approach, promoted by @sadler2010, provides several advantages:

- **Higher Statistical Power**: when the measurement range is narrow, the joint region can need several-fold (sometimes far) fewer samples than the two confidence intervals to detect the same bias
- **Accounts for Parameter Correlation**: When the measurement range is narrow, slope and intercept are highly negatively correlated
- **More Appropriate Test**: Testing against a point (e.g., slope=1, intercept=0) is naturally done with a region, not separate intervals

The power advantage is most pronounced when the ratio of maximum to minimum X values is small (< 10:1), which is common in clinical method comparisons.

Two regions are available through the `method` argument:

- **`"sadler"`** (default for Deming regression): the sum-of-squares region of @sadler2010. It uses the Deming sum of squares directly, not a variance-covariance matrix, and is not exactly an ellipse. In simulations it rejected a true identity line 4.3-5.9% of the time at a nominal 5%, from n = 10 upward.
- **`"wald"`** (the only option for Passing-Bablok regression): an ellipse from the variance-covariance matrix of the estimates. For Deming regression that matrix is a delete-one jackknife, and the test is liberal in small samples (about 8.5% at n = 10 and 7.4% at n = 20 at a nominal 5%). For Passing-Bablok regression, use bootstrap or delete-d jackknife resampling (both held about 5% in simulations).

## Visualizing the Joint Confidence Region

The `plot_joint()` function allows visualization of the confidence region in parameter space:

```{r}
plot_joint(dem1, 
           ideal_slope = 1, 
           ideal_intercept = 0,
           show_intervals = TRUE)
```

This plot shows:

- The **red curve**: Joint confidence region (Sadler's region by default; `method = "wald"` draws the ellipse)
- The **blue rectangle**: Traditional confidence intervals
- The **black dot**: Estimated (intercept, slope)
- The **green/red X**: Ideal point (whether enclosed or not)

Notice how the region is narrower than the rectangle, especially in the directions that matter for detecting bias.

For Passing-Bablok regression, bootstrap (or delete-d jackknife) resampling must be used to obtain the variance-covariance matrix needed for the joint confidence region:

```{r}
plot_joint(pb2)
```

## Joint Hypothesis Test

The `joint_test()` function provides a formal hypothesis test for whether the identity line (slope = 1, intercept = 0) falls within the joint confidence region:

```{r}
joint_test(dem1)
```

This returns an `htest` object with Sadler's F statistic and p-value. The Wald version (Mahalanobis distance) is available with `joint_test(dem1, method = "wald")`. The test can also be applied to Passing-Bablok models fitted with bootstrap, where it is always the Wald test:

```{r}
joint_test(pb2)
```

# Theoretical Details

## Deming Calculative Approach

Deming regression assumes paired measures ($x_i, \space  y_i$) are each measured with error.

$$
x_i = X_i + \epsilon_i
$$

$$
y_i = Y_i + \delta_i
$$

We can then measure the relationship between the two variables with the following model.

$$
\hat Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \hat X_i
$$

Traditionally there are 2 null hypotheses.

First, the intercept is equal to zero:

$$
H_0: \beta_0 = 0 \space vs. \space H_1: \beta_0 \ne 0
$$

Second, that the slope is equal to one:

$$
H_0: \beta_1 = 1 \space vs. \space H_1: \beta_1 \ne 1
$$

# Joint Confidence Region Calculative Approach

## Sadler's region (Deming regression, default)

Deming regression with error ratio $\lambda$ and weights $w_i$ minimises

$$
S(a, b) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{w_i (y_i - a - b x_i)^2}{1 + \lambda b^2}
$$

Following @sadler2010 (after Draper and Smith), with $\hat S$ the minimum, the joint $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence region for $(\beta_0, \beta_1)$ is the set of $(a, b)$ with

$$
F = \frac{(S(a, b) - \hat S)/2}{\hat S / (n - 2)} \leq F_{2, n-2, 1-\alpha}
$$

and the joint test of a hypothesized $(a_0, b_0)$ (e.g., $(0, 1)$ for identity) compares $F$ at that point with the $F(2, n - 2)$ distribution. No variance-covariance matrix is needed, and only the error ratio (not the size of the errors) matters. For a fixed slope the condition is quadratic in the intercept, so the region is drawn exactly.

## Wald ellipse

This was my original solution for this joint testing problem. I would, for Deming regression, stick with Sadler's region.

With `method = "wald"` the region is

$$
(\hat{\beta} - \beta_0)^T V^{-1} (\hat{\beta} - \beta_0) \leq 2 F_{2, n-2, 1-\alpha}
$$

(or $\chi^2_{2, 1-\alpha}$ with `test_method = "asymptotic"`), where:

- $\hat{\beta}$ = estimated parameters $(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1)$
- $\beta_0$ = hypothesized parameters (e.g., $(0, 1)$ for identity)
- $V$ = variance-covariance matrix (jackknife for Deming; bootstrap or delete-d jackknife for Passing-Bablok)

This forms an ellipse in parameter space that accounts for the correlation between slope and intercept.

## Measurement Error

A Deming regression model also assumes the measurement error ($\sigma^2$) ratio is constant. In `SimplyAgree`, the error ratio is always the error variance of x divided by the error variance of y.

$$
\lambda = \frac{\sigma^2_\epsilon}{\sigma^2_\delta} 
$$

In `SimplyAgree`, the error ratio can be set with the `error.ratio` argument. It defaults to 1, but can be changed by the user. If replicate measures are taken, then the user can use the `id` argument to indicate which measures belong to which subject/participant. The measurement error, and the error ratio, will then be estimated from the data itself.

If the data was not measured in replicate then the error ratio ($\lambda$) can be estimated from the coefficient of variation (if that data is available) and the mean of x and y ($\bar x, \space \bar y$).

$$
\lambda = \frac{(CV_x \cdot \bar x)^2}{(CV_y \cdot \bar y)^2}
$$

## Weights

In some cases the variance of X and Y may increase proportional to the true value of the measure. In these cases, it may be prudent to use "weighted" Deming regression models. The weights used in `SimplyAgree` are the same as those suggested by @linnet1993.

$$
\hat w_i = \frac{1}{ [ \frac{x_i + \lambda \cdot y_i}{1 + \lambda}]^2}
$$

Weights can also be provided through the `weights` argument. If weighted Deming regression is not selected (`weighted = FALSE`), the weights for each observation is equal to 1.

The estimated mean of X and Y are then estimated as the following.

$$
\bar x_w =  \frac{\Sigma^{N}_{i=1} \hat w_i \cdot x_i}{\Sigma^{N}_{i=1} \hat w_i}
$$

$$
\bar y_w =  \frac{\Sigma^{N}_{i=1} \hat w_i \cdot y_i}{\Sigma^{N}_{i=1} \hat w_i}
$$

## Estimating the Slope and Intercept

First, there are 3 components ($v_x, \space v_y, \space cov_{xy}$)

$$
v_x = \Sigma_{i=1}^N \space \hat w_i \cdot (x_i- \bar x_w)^2
$$
$$
v_y = \Sigma_{i=1}^N \space \hat w_i \cdot (y_i- \bar y_w)^2
$$
$$
cov_{xy} = \Sigma_{i=1}^N \space \hat w_i \cdot  (x_i- \bar x_w) \cdot (y_i- \bar y_w)
$$

The slope ($b_1$) can then be estimated with the following equation.

$$
b_1 = \frac{(\lambda \cdot v_y - v_x) + \sqrt{(v_x-\lambda \cdot v_y)^2 + 4 \cdot \lambda \cdot cov_{xy}^2}}{2 \cdot \lambda \cdot cov_{xy}}
$$

The intercept ($b_0$) can then be estimated with the following equation.

$$
b_0 = \bar y_w - b_1 \cdot \bar x_w
$$

The standard errors of b1 and b0 are both estimated using a jackknife method (detailed by @linnet1990).
